content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 17: Business Logic, Concurrency, and Workflow Security. It builds practical understanding of Financial and External Transaction Integrity with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Financial and External Transaction Integrity makes secure behavior repeatable across implementation, dependencies, configuration, and release. Verify the provider signature over the exact received payload, enforce freshness where supported, and use an idempotent event record so replayed callbacks cannot repeat side effects.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Financial and External Transaction Integrity can be understood through this sequence: Define invariant → Model concurrent retries → Commit atomically → Test duplicate + race. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 128.1 Payment provider verification; 128.2 Server-side transaction amount calculation; 128.3 Verified webhooks versus browser redirects; 128.4 Duplicate event handling; 128.5 Reconciliation and audit trails; 128.6 Preventing invalid or contradictory financial states. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Verify the provider signature over the exact received payload, enforce freshness where supported, and use an idempotent event record so replayed callbacks cannot repeat side effects. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.
